html:
The third Islamic caliphate, ruled by a dynasty descended from Muhammad's uncle Abbas. It ran from 750 to 1258, from Iraq, with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time.

The Abbasids came to power in a revolution that started in Khurasan, in eastern Iran, and overthrew the Umayyads of Damascus. Moving the centre east, to Iraq, tilted the empire toward Persian ways of government. In 762 the caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad, a round city on the Tigris that soon became one of the largest cities in the world.

The first century was the high point:

  • Under Harun al-Rashid and his son al-Mamun, Baghdad drew scholars, money and trade from Spain to China.
  • Greek science and philosophy were translated into Arabic, with Persian and Indian works too.
  • Al-Khwarizmi wrote on algebra, and Indian numerals came into use.
  • Paper, made at Samarkand after 751 and soon in Baghdad, made books cheap.

After about 900 real power drained away. Provinces went their own way: the Umayyads in Spain, the Fatimids in Egypt, the Samanids in the east. In 945 the Buyids, a Persian family, took Baghdad, and in 1055 the Seljuk Turks replaced them. The caliph stayed as a religious figurehead who gave rulers their legitimacy.

In 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad and killed the last caliph there. A line of shadow caliphs lived on in Cairo under the Mamluks until the Ottoman conquest of 1517.
sum: The third Islamic caliphate, ruled by a dynasty descended from Muhammad's uncle Abbas. It ran from 750 to 1258, from Iraq, with Baghdad as its capital for most of that time.
